title: Why rich countries feel poor
intro: Four countries, one puzzle. Prompted by a popular explainer and checked against other sources.
bannerHeadline: Why rich countries feel poor: homes, care and the limits of growth
bannerDeck: A video’s argument, checked against housing, childcare, pay and sentiment data in four countries.
ourViewIntro: Donna Daily’s own analysis of the argument, setting out more than one side and drawing on the linked reporting. It is not an endorsement of the video.
notes: This is a Donna Daily special edition on why people in rich countries feel poorer than headline numbers suggest. It does not replace the daily edition.

The edition was prompted by a public YouTube explainer, “The Worrying Reason Rich Countries Feel Poor Now” by OBF. Its argument is summarized and attributed to it. Its figures are labelled as the video’s unless another story re-checks them against an independent source.

Donna Daily then researched the topic independently using official statistics (ONS, Statistics Canada, University of Michigan), research centers and think tanks (Harvard JCHS, Opportunity Insights, Resolution Foundation, C.D. Howe, IMF, NBER), bank economists (Desjardins, RBC, CIBC) and news reporting (NBC News, CNN, the Guardian, NPR, Pew, YouGov).
Price-to-income ratios differ by source: some compare prices with household income, others with one full-time worker’s earnings. Ratios are only compared within the same source.

Opinion is split in two: “Our view” pieces are Donna Daily’s own analysis, written to present more than one side; “What columnists are arguing” paraphrases named writers at other outlets, with links to the originals.
provenance: Research pages were opened on Nov. 5, 2026, between about 11:15 and 11:30 AM ET. Individual check times were not logged, so none are shown on the story checks.

The IMF blog refused automated access. Its figures were confirmed from search-index excerpts of the IMF blog and working paper, and the story check says so. The Free Press and The Dispatch are partly paywalled, so only their free portions were read.
Some sources are older than this edition, including Chetty’s mobility study (2016–17), the Summers paper (2024) and a July 2025 report on German contributions. They are dated on each story.
Photos are from Wikimedia Commons under free licences or the public domain. They were checked on their file pages, cropped to 16:9 and credited under each picture. All are file photos.

stories.headline: Cheap TVs, dear homes: why rich countries feel poor
stories.glance: The thesis: goods got cheap; homes, care and time didn’t
stories.deck: Factory goods got far cheaper; homes near good jobs and care did not. Independent data back much of that story, but not all of it.
stories.summary: A widely shared explainer from the YouTube channel OBF argues that rich economies are very good at making factory goods plentiful and bad at making land near good jobs, or people’s time, plentiful. Donna Daily checked the core claims against other sources. On housing, they largely hold. Harvard’s Joint Center for Housing Studies puts the typical US home at 4.7 times median household income in 2025, against an average of 3.2 in the 1990s. Britain’s statistics office says a typical home in England costs 7.6 times full-time earnings, roughly double the 1997 ratio. On care, Child Care Aware of America puts average US child care at $13,184 a year, about 10% of a two-parent household’s median income. The mood fits too. Michigan’s consumer sentiment index was 48.0 in October, 10% below a year earlier, and a Harris poll for the Guardian found 61% of Americans wrongly believe the US is already in recession. Two cautions apply. English and US price-to-income ratios have eased since 2021–22. And part of this year’s gloom comes from a fresh shock, the Iran war’s energy spike, rather than from decades of scarcity.
stories.why: If the squeeze is about scarce homes and care rather than money printing or greed, the fixes are slower and more political: planning, building and how care is paid for.
stories.label: Analysis
stories.note: The video uses its own price-to-income measure (household income); Harvard JCHS and the ONS use different definitions, so their numbers are not directly comparable with each other or with the video’s.

stories.headline: The explainer’s case: no single villain, just scarce land and scarce time
stories.glance: The video tests six popular explanations
stories.deck: OBF’s video tests six popular explanations across four countries and finds that none fits all of them alone. Its answer is that rich economies leave land near jobs, and people’s time, scarce.
stories.summary: The video starts from a paradox: many people in rich countries expect their children to be worse off, even as official growth forecasts rise. It then compares the US, Britain, Canada and Germany. Since 2000, it says, goods such as televisions have become far cheaper in hours of work, but housing has not. By its count, a home cost about three years of household income around 1990, against about 4.5 in the US, 5.2 in Britain and 5.4 in Canada today. Care is the second big cost: nursery and university in Britain, health insurance in the US, an incomplete $10-a-day childcare program in Canada, and in Germany near-free university paid for through high social contributions. It then tests six suspects: money printing and post-2022 inflation, a “vibecession,” weak wages, greedy companies, boomers and taxes. Each explains part of the picture, it argues, but none explains all four countries. It leaves immigration out so that all four countries are compared on the same terms. Its conclusion is that productivity growth makes manufactured goods abundant but cannot easily make land or caring time abundant, a version of economist William Baumol’s “cost disease.” Each country then adds its own twist: inequality in the US, stagnant pay in Britain, decline relative to the US and household debt in Canada, and care costs hidden in payroll charges in Germany.
stories.why: It is a clear, testable framework. The rest of this edition checks its main numbers against other sources and sets out where economists disagree.
stories.label: Analysis
stories.note: This is a summary of the video’s own argument. Figures here are the video’s unless another story in this edition re-checks them.

stories.headline: US homes cost nearly five years of income, against about three in the 1990s
stories.glance: US: homes 4.7× income (3.2× in the 1990s)
stories.deck: Harvard’s housing center says the price-to-income ratio has hovered near five for five years, and the monthly payment on a typical home has nearly doubled since 2020.
stories.summary: The Joint Center for Housing Studies’ 2026 report says the median existing single-family home sold for 4.7 times median household income in 2025. That is down slightly from a record 5.0 in 2022 but up from 4.1 in 2019 and an average of 3.2 in the 1990s. Prices are up 54% nationally since 2020, or almost 25% after inflation. The monthly mortgage payment on a median-priced home, assuming 3.5% down and a 30-year fixed rate, was about $2,420 at the end of 2025, nearly double the $1,240 at the end of 2020, when rates were near record lows. There are signs of cooling: annual price growth slowed to 0.7% in February 2026, and 41 of the 100 largest metros saw outright declines in early 2026. The video’s figure of about 4.5 years of income is close to the center’s, though the two use different data.
stories.why: High prices and higher rates together are what lock people out. A fall in rates alone, the report notes, has given buyers only modest relief.

stories.headline: An English home costs 7.6 years of pay, about double 1997, though it has eased since 2021
stories.glance: England: homes 7.6× pay, double 1997
stories.deck: Official figures show affordability improving as pay outpaces prices, but London remains far out of reach and private renters on lower incomes spend a large share of income on rent.
stories.summary: Britain’s Office for National Statistics says the median home in England, at £300,000, cost 7.6 times median full-time earnings in 2025, the lowest ratio since 2015, down from 7.8 in 2024. Since the 2021 peak, earnings have risen 25% while median prices have risen 5%. Over the long run the picture is starker: in 1997, a typical home in England and Wales cost three to four times a full-time salary. London stands at 10.6, and Kensington and Chelsea at 25.2. The ONS treats five times earnings as a broad affordability threshold. The Resolution Foundation, a think tank, says about 8.6 million lower-income Britons now rent privately, spending on average 43% of disposable income on housing. The ONS measures against one full-time worker’s earnings, while the video uses household income, which explains the gap between 7.6 and the video’s 5.2.
stories.why: Britain shows that improving affordability is possible, through pay rises outpacing prices, but also how far it has to go.
stories.label: Official figures

stories.headline: In Toronto and Vancouver, renting is becoming permanent for the middle class
stories.glance: Canada: “the permanent renter” in global cities
stories.deck: Desjardins economists say the two cities now behave like London or New York, and RBC warns that a year of easing affordability may be ending as rates rise.
stories.summary: In an April 2026 study, Desjardins senior economist Kari Norman argues that Toronto and Vancouver increasingly resemble “global cities,” where home prices partly decouple from national incomes. Restoring broad homeownership there could now appear infeasible, she writes, given the size of the income, price or rate changes it would take. Long-term renting is spreading into the professional middle class, and the rental stock lacks family-sized units. RBC Economics says its national affordability measure, the share of a typical household’s income needed to cover ownership costs, was 52.8% in the second quarter of 2026. That was little changed, and the smallest improvement in almost a year. RBC adds that rising bond yields and possible Bank of Canada rate hikes next year could push ownership costs up again. The video says a Canadian home costs about 5.4 years of household income, the highest of its four countries. Donna Daily did not find a matching official figure on the same basis.
stories.why: Canada has the biggest housing gap of the four. What happens to rates in 2027 may matter as much as new supply.
stories.label: Analysis

stories.headline: Why care keeps getting pricier: the “cost disease” behind nurseries and hospitals
stories.glance: Baumol: why care costs outrun goods
stories.deck: When factories get more productive, wages rise everywhere. A nursery worker can’t care for many more toddlers, so care costs rise relative to goods. Economists argue over how much this explains.
stories.summary: The idea comes from the economist William Baumol. A string quartet takes as many players today as it did in 1800, but musicians’ pay has to keep pace with pay in industries where productivity soared. The same goes for childcare, nursing and teaching. George Mason economist Alex Tabarrok, co-author of a book on the effect, compared US price data and found that over 26 years the price of day care and preschool rose 36% relative to overall prices, while pet care, which is far less regulated, rose 28%. He argues that the similarity means regulation such as staff ratios is not the main driver of the slow, steady rise, though he accepts that regulation raises the level of prices. Other researchers put more weight on rules, workforce requirements and subsidies, and empirical tests of Baumol in health care have produced mixed results. The OBF video uses Baumol as half of its answer.
stories.why: If Baumol is right, care will keep getting relatively more expensive as countries get richer. The question becomes who pays, not how to make it cheap.
stories.label: Analysis

stories.headline: Childcare: high US prices, English subsidies and Canadian waitlists
stories.glance: Childcare: $13,184 in the US; waitlists in Canada
stories.deck: Three countries are trying three different ways to pay for childcare. Each shows a different trade-off.
stories.summary: United States: Child Care Aware of America says the average annual price was $13,184 in 2025, 10% of median income for a two-parent household and 33% for a single parent. In every state with data, center care for two children costs more than median rent. Britain: Coram’s 2026 survey says the price of a part-time nursery place for an under-two in England nearly tripled from £55 a week in 2001 to £160 in 2024. Expanded funded hours have since cut the cost of a full-time place by 39% for eligible working parents, but prices rose 5% in Scotland and 8% in Wales. Canada: the C.D. Howe Institute says eight provinces and territories have reached average fees of $10 a day or less and the rest have at least halved them, but waitlists are growing. More than three-quarters of centers reported waitlists in 2024. Ottawa said in a briefing note that more than 125,000 of a targeted 250,000 new spaces had been created by October 2025, against a March 2026 deadline.
stories.why: Lower fees help families who get a place. Without more staff and spaces, the shortage moves from price to availability, which Baumol’s logic would predict.
stories.label: Reported

stories.headline: Germany’s care bill is paid through the payslip, and it is rising
stories.glance: Germany: social contributions ~42% of gross pay
stories.deck: Nursery fees are low and university is nearly free, the video notes. But health, care, pension and jobless insurance together take about 42% of gross pay, split between worker and employer.
stories.summary: Germany funds much of what the video calls “care” through social insurance contributions, split roughly equally between employers and workers. In July 2025, tagesschau reported that combined contributions were already about 42% of gross pay. Government economic adviser Martin Werding said the total would reach 50% at some point without reform as the population ages, and could hit 45% by the end of the current parliament. A payroll reference site lists the combined 2027 rate at 42.3%, including an average health top-up of 2.9%. The video argues that this is where Germany’s squeeze hides: families pay little at the nursery door but see it in net pay, while the economy stalled in 2023–25.
stories.why: Germany shows the cost of care doesn’t vanish when it is collectivized. It moves from fees to payroll, where it weighs on take-home pay and hiring.
stories.label: Reported
stories.note: Werding’s figures are forecasts, not current rates. The 2027 rate comes from a payroll reference site and partly reflects planned changes.

stories.headline: Americans’ mood sits near historic lows as the Iran war lifts fuel prices
stories.glance: US sentiment 48.0; 61% think it’s a recession
stories.deck: Sentiment is 15% below February, just before the Iran conflict began. Inflation rose to 3.7% in September, and paychecks have not kept up since March.
stories.summary: The University of Michigan’s sentiment index was 48.0 in October, 10.4% below a year earlier. Its director said sentiment is 15% lower than in February, just before the Iran conflict, and that purchasing power dominates consumers’ views. The November preliminary reading is scheduled for Friday at 10 AM ET. NBC News reported that consumer prices rose 3.7% in the year to September, with gasoline accounting for over half of the monthly increase. Wages were growing about 3% a year, and paychecks have not outpaced inflation since March. Moody’s Analytics estimates the war has cost the average household about $2,000, CNN reported. In polls, YouGov found 49% of Americans call the economy poor, the most since July 2022. Pew found that 70% have cut back on extras in the past year. A Harris poll for the Guardian found that 61% wrongly think the US is already in recession.
stories.why: This year’s gloom has a concrete new cause on top of the long-run squeeze. That matters because energy shocks can fade, while housing and care costs don’t.
stories.label: Reported

stories.headline: The “vibecession” may be partly a measurement gap: inflation figures leave out the cost of borrowing
stories.glance: Summers: borrowing costs explain much of the gloom
stories.deck: Research co-written by Larry Summers finds that adding interest costs to inflation explains about three-quarters of 2023’s gap between US sentiment and the official numbers. An IMF study adds a second partial explanation for the 2022 surge.
stories.summary: In an NBER working paper, Marijn Bolhuis, Judd Cramer, Karl Oskar Schulz and Lawrence Summers argue that the official consumer price index has left out mortgage interest since a 1983 redesign. It therefore misses the pain of higher rates on mortgages, car loans and credit cards. Adding those costs accounts for almost three-quarters of the 2023 gap between US consumer sentiment and what unemployment and inflation would predict. Across ten rich economies, sentiment gaps tracked rises in interest rates and were large in Germany, Spain and Austria. On the separate “greedy companies” theory, a 2023 IMF study found that domestic profits accounted for about 45% of euro-area inflation from early 2022 to early 2023. Import prices accounted for about 40% and labor costs for about 25%. Both explain a recent surge. As the video notes, neither explains why housing and care costs have been climbing for decades.
stories.why: When people say things feel worse than the data show, they may be partly right about the data. Rate rises hit borrowers in ways the headline inflation rate doesn’t capture.
stories.label: Analysis

stories.headline: The $140,000 “poverty line”: wrong numbers, but a real feeling
stories.glance: The $140k “poverty line” debate
stories.deck: A viral essay claimed a family of four needs $140,000 to escape poverty. Economists took the math apart, but asked why it felt true. Research on relative income suggests an answer.
stories.summary: Michael Green, a Wall Street strategist, argued on Substack and in The Free Press that participating in basic American life now costs about $140,000 a year for a family of four, against an official poverty line of about $31,200. Critics including Tyler Cowen, Scott Winship and Cato’s Scott Lincicome said the figure rests on one of the country’s priciest counties, Essex County in New Jersey, and treats typical spending as a survival minimum. Quartz noted that the same method gives about $94,000 in Lynchburg, Virginia. Reason reported that Green later conceded his math and geography were flawed and said his real point was that families feel more stretched. Lincicome’s answer is psychology: the “hedonic treadmill,” where expectations rise with incomes. That echoes the Easterlin paradox: richer people are happier than poorer people at any one time, but countries don’t get happier as they get richer, largely because people compare themselves with others. The video adds Fred Hirsch’s idea of “positional goods,” such as a home in the best school district, which can’t multiply with growth.
stories.why: Both things can be true: the $140,000 figure is wrong, and the standard of a “normal” middle-class life has become harder to reach.
stories.label: Analysis

stories.headline: A coin flip: only half of Americans born in the 1980s out-earn their parents
stories.glance: US: 90% out-earned parents (1940s) vs 50% (1980s)
stories.deck: Raj Chetty’s team found the share fell from about 90% for children born in the 1940s, mostly because growth has been shared less evenly.
stories.summary: Researchers led by Raj Chetty used census and tax records to compare children’s household incomes at 30 with their parents’ at the same age, adjusted for inflation, taxes and household size. About 90% of children born in 1940 out-earned their parents, compared with about 50% of those born in the 1980s. The largest declines were in the middle class and in the industrial Midwest. The authors found the decline is driven mainly by a more unequal distribution of growth, not slower growth. The video uses this as America’s twist: the US economy grew faster than its peers, but fewer people felt it. The data stop with the 1984 birth cohort and predate the pandemic and this year’s energy shock.
stories.why: It explains why the US can top growth tables and still feel stuck. The question is who gets the gains, not just how big they are.
stories.label: Reported

stories.headline: Britain’s lower-income half has seen two decades of near-flat living standards
stories.glance: UK: poorer half’s incomes +0.5% a year since mid-2000s
stories.deck: The Resolution Foundation says incomes for the poorer half of working-age households have grown 0.5% a year since the mid-2000s, after doubling in the 40 years before.
stories.summary: The think tank’s “Unsung Britain” project says the 13 million working-age families in the bottom half of the income distribution are working more than before, and the minimum wage has cut low pay sharply. Yet their typical disposable incomes have grown just 0.5% a year since the mid-2000s. In the 40 years to 2004–05, incomes for similar families doubled. Three-quarters of the real earnings growth for below-middle-income families since the mid-1990s came before 2005. Its 2026 Living Standards Outlook projects a one-year boost of 4.7% for these families in 2026–27, from above-inflation benefit rises and the end of the two-child limit. After that, weak real wages, frozen tax thresholds and rising council tax and housing costs are likely to mean stagnation again. The video calls Britain’s pay record a “failure.” The data support that for the long run, though the Foundation also credits the narrowing of low pay.
stories.why: In Britain, weak pay growth explains much of the gloom. That distinguishes it from the US, where growth was strong but unevenly shared.
stories.label: Analysis

stories.headline: Canada is slipping behind the US, though not as far as the headline numbers suggest
stories.glance: Canada: output per person 14% behind US trend
stories.deck: Statistics Canada says Canada’s output per person has fallen 14% relative to the US since 1997, mostly because of weak productivity. A bank analysis says median workers have held up better.
stories.summary: A March 2026 Statistics Canada study finds that Canadian labour productivity has fallen 26% relative to the US since the late 1990s. Real GDP per person in the third quarter of 2025 was 14% lower relative to the US than in early 1997. Until about 2015, high commodity prices and longer hours hid the gap. Since the oil price collapse they no longer do, and the authors call weak productivity growth “the principal reason” Canada is falling behind. CIBC economists offer a counterpoint. Measured in current prices, the per-person gap is smaller, and median weekly earnings for full-time workers grew more in Canada than in the US after 2000. A Bank of Canada study found that the top 10% of earners account for up to two-thirds of the productivity gap. CIBC still finds the gains wiped out over the past decade. The video also cites Canada’s high household debt, which Donna Daily did not re-verify.
stories.why: Canadians compare themselves with Americans. A widening gap at the top and rising housing costs can make the country feel poorer even where median pay has kept pace.
stories.label: Official figures + Analysis

stories.headline: Germany’s economy is recovering, slowly, after years of stalling
stories.glance: Germany: 1.3% growth forecast for 2026
stories.deck: The leading institutes forecast 1.3% growth this year, helped by exports and the Iran war’s hit to Gulf competitors, but high energy prices are squeezing households.
stories.summary: Germany’s leading economic institutes, in their joint autumn forecast, say the economy has been recovering since the end of 2025, faster than expected in spring. They forecast growth of 1.3% in 2026, 1.1% in 2027 and 0.4% in 2028. Exports and manufacturing rose in the first half, helped by the global AI boom and by production disruptions at Gulf competitors during the Iran war. Growth nearly stalled in the third quarter, at an estimated 0.1%, as low river levels hurt the chemical industry. Higher energy prices are weighing on purchasing power and consumption. Inflation is expected to rise from 2.8% this year to 3.2% in 2027, and employment to keep falling for now. The institutes also warn that the budget deficit is rising. The video’s description of a stalled economy fits 2023–25. This year’s data show a modest, fragile recovery.
stories.why: Growth alone won’t ease Germany’s squeeze if energy costs and payroll contributions keep rising faster than take-home pay.
stories.label: Forecast

stories.author: Donna Daily
stories.headline: The squeeze is real, but it is not everywhere, and it is not everything
stories.glance: Our view: real squeeze, but not the whole story
stories.deck: Housing and care explain the long-run pinch better than money printing or greed. But some indicators are improving, and this year’s energy shock is a separate problem.
stories.summary: The case for the video’s diagnosis is strong. Independent figures from Harvard’s housing center and Britain’s statistics office show homes costing roughly twice as many years of pay as a generation ago. Childcare costs have outpaced inflation for 25 years in England and now rival rent in the US. Neither inflation since 2022 nor company profits can explain trends that started decades earlier. The case for caution is also real. England’s ratio has improved four years running as pay outpaced prices. The US ratio is off its 2022 peak, and prices fell in 41 big metros early this year. Much of the current American gloom has a recent and possibly temporary cause: the Iran war pushed gasoline up from about $2.98 to over $4 a gallon, and Michigan’s index fell 15% from February. Our read: there are two problems. One is structural (scarce homes and care) and needs years of building and reform. The other is cyclical (energy and borrowing costs) and could ease faster. Treating them as one problem risks the wrong remedies for both.
stories.why: Voters just punished incumbents over prices. What politicians think caused the squeeze will shape what they promise to fix.
stories.label: Our view

stories.author: Donna Daily
stories.headline: Subsidies without supply just move the queue
stories.glance: Our view: build supply before subsidising demand
stories.deck: Canada, England and Germany each cut what families pay at the door. Canada’s waitlists show what happens when the places don’t follow.
stories.summary: Cutting fees is popular and quick. Canada has brought childcare to $10 a day or close to it in most provinces, and England’s funded hours have cut full-time nursery costs by 39% for eligible families. But the C.D. Howe Institute finds that the main barrier in Canada has shifted “from affordability to availability.” Ottawa had created about half its targeted new spaces by October 2025. Germany shows that collectivizing care costs moves them onto payslips, where contributions near 42% of gross pay. Housing follows the same logic: subsidies to buyers in a market short of homes mostly raise prices. The strongest argument on the other side comes from Baumol himself, as Alex Tabarrok puts it: care getting relatively dearer is a sign that the rest of the economy is getting more productive, and richer societies can afford it. Our read: Tabarrok is right that care will never get cheap, which is exactly why it has to be planned for and staffed. Fee cuts without more workers, spaces and homes will keep producing waitlists.
stories.why: Canada, Britain and Germany are all debating more spending on care and housing. Supply, not fee cuts, will decide whether families feel the difference.
stories.label: Our view

stories.author: Donna Daily
stories.headline: “It’s just expectations” is half an answer
stories.glance: Our view: expectations matter, but mobility fell
stories.deck: Economists are right that the $140,000 poverty line is bad math and that people compare themselves with others. That does not make the decline in getting ahead imaginary.
stories.summary: The critics’ case is solid. Green’s $140,000 relies on one of America’s priciest counties, and he later conceded the math. The Easterlin research shows that in rich countries, faster income growth hasn’t produced measurably happier populations, partly because people compare themselves with others. Some of what feels like poverty is the rising standard of a “normal” life. But expectations aren’t the whole story. Chetty’s data show that a 1980s-born American has only about an even chance of out-earning their parents, compared with nine in ten for those born in 1940. The Resolution Foundation shows Britain’s poorer half running in place for 20 years. And a home in a good school district is, as Hirsch argued, a positional good that growth can’t multiply. Our read: telling people their gloom is a vibe will not persuade anyone. Expecting your grandparents’ one-income life is unrealistic. Expecting to do better than your parents is a promise rich countries used to keep, and some no longer do.
stories.why: How leaders describe the problem, as perception or as reality, affects whether voters trust anything else they say about the economy.
stories.label: Our view

stories.author: Eric Boehm
stories.headline: “The poverty line isn’t a vibe”
stories.glance: Reason: feeling stretched isn’t poverty
stories.deck: Boehm argues that critics were right to dismiss the $140,000 figure, and that redefining poverty to mean “middle-class trade-offs” misreads the economy.
stories.summary: Boehm writes that Green retreated from the $140,000 figure, conceding flaws in his math and geography, but kept the claim that middle-class families feel too stretched for official measures to mean anything. Boehm says the poverty line was never a gateway to the middle class, and that not every family can afford the median apartment, by definition. Real poverty, he writes, looks like the roughly 14% of American children in overcrowded homes. He also criticizes the “Cost of Thriving Index” that Green relied on. Citing Scott Winship, he says that once taxes, family subsidies and women’s earnings are counted, the cost of thriving has fallen since 1985.
stories.why: This is the strongest case that the squeeze, while real, is being overstated by bad measures.
stories.label: Opinion

stories.author: Alex Tabarrok
stories.headline: Day care costs rise for the same reason dog boarding does
stories.glance: Tabarrok: blame Baumol, not regulation
stories.deck: Tabarrok compares childcare with lightly regulated pet care and finds similar real price rises, evidence that productivity elsewhere, not rules, drives care costs.
stories.summary: Tabarrok notes that boarding his dog in northern Virginia costs about as much as a Motel 6. Over 26 years, he finds, the real price of day care and preschool rose 36%, while pet services rose 28%. Because pet care is far less regulated, he argues, regulation probably isn’t what drives the slow rise in childcare costs, though he agrees it raises the price level. He points to research finding that vet spending is rising about as fast as human health spending, despite very different rules. His conclusion is that when productivity rises in other industries and stays flat in care, care’s relative price must rise.
stories.why: It is a clear, data-based case for the Baumol half of the video’s argument, from one of the economists who wrote the book on it.
stories.label: Opinion

stories.author: Phil Mattingly
stories.headline: What “affordability” means to the people living it
stories.glance: CNN: the deal of “work hard, buy a home” is fraying
stories.deck: After three dozen interviews in four cities, Mattingly argues that big costs such as housing and childcare are breaking an old promise, even as top-line economic data look strong.
stories.summary: Mattingly writes that he spent months with economic data before traveling to Cleveland, Boston, Atlanta and elsewhere. He describes a single mother outside Cleveland whose rent rose from $785 to nearly $1,600 for the same unit in seven years while her income stayed flat, and a Boston-area couple earning $150,000 with three children under four. His argument is that the squeeze is no longer occasional bad luck. Big costs such as housing, childcare and a thinning retirement floor are rising until families are one flat tire from trouble. Meanwhile corporate earnings and spending by better-off households stay strong. He calls “affordability” a word that flattens real people into talking points.
stories.why: It is the strongest on-the-ground case that the gloom reflects real change, not just perception.
stories.label: Opinion
